how_to_obtain.instruction: On FortiGate, list all configured syslog server destinations across all syslogd instances.
how_to_obtain.command: for i in 1 2 3 4; do echo "=== syslogd$i ==="; show log syslogd${i} setting | grep -E 'status|server|port'; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each active syslogd instance shows 'status: enable' and a valid 'server' IP. Instances with 'status: disable' or no server IP are non-functional destinations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Palo Alto PAN-OS, navigate to Device > Server Profiles > Syslog and list all defined server profiles, noting the server name, IP address, and port for each entry.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Device > Server Profiles > Syslog
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table of syslog server profiles each with a valid IP address and port number (typically UDP/514 or TCP/6514). An empty table with forwarding nominally enabled confirms zero valid destinations.

typical_values: [] (empty — misconfiguration when forwarding is nominally enabled)

option_description: Controls whether firewall logs are retained exclusively on the local filesystem with no forwarding configured to remote destinations such as a SIEM, syslog server, or log aggregator.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags this as a 'Log Forwarding Misconfiguration Or Absence' exposure when local_only_log_storage is true. Local-only logs create a single point of failure: if the firewall is compromised, an attacker can alter or destroy all audit evidence. Without centralized forwarding, there is no independent copy of traffic events, denies, or rule changes available for incident response or compliance review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based firewalls using rsyslog or syslog-ng, check whether any remote forwarding targets are configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of '@@<remote-host>' or 'omfwd' entries indicates forwarding is configured; absence confirms local-only storage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the firewall's logging configuration file for remote syslog or SIEM destination entries.
how_to_obtain.file_path: /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf or /etc/ufw/ufw.conf or vendor-specific path (e.g., /config/system/syslog on Vyos)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If no remote IP/hostname and port entries are present under logging stanzas, log storage is local only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the firewall management console logging settings and verify whether any remote syslog, SIEM, or log forwarding destinations are defined and enabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management Console > Logging > Log Forwarding / Remote Syslog Settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An empty destination list or all forwarding toggles set to disabled confirms local_only_log_storage is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the firewall management API for the current log forwarding configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An empty or absent log-forwarding element confirms no remote destinations are configured.

typical_values: true (logs stored locally only — common in smaller deployments without centralized logging infrastructure)
false (log forwarding configured to SIEM or syslog server — recommended secure posture)

option_description: Indicates whether the firewall management interface enforces role-based access control, enabling administrators to be assigned differentiated roles such as read-only, rule-editor, or auditor rather than all accounts sharing a single super-admin role.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Excessive Administrative Privilege Assignment' immediately when rbac_enabled is false, regardless of other settings. Without RBAC, every administrator has unrestricted access to all firewall functions. A single compromised credential then provides full control over rule sets, logging, and configuration — maximizing the blast radius of any credential theft or insider threat.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log into the firewall management interface and navigate to the user management or administrator settings to check whether role definitions beyond a single admin type are present and assignable.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management Console > Device > Administrators > Roles (or equivalent vendor path)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Multiple named roles (e.g., auditor, rule-editor, read-only) listed and assignable to accounts indicates RBAC is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On firewall devices accessible via CLI, list configured admin roles to determine if RBAC differentiation is active.
how_to_obtain.command: show admin-role all; show admins; show running-config | section role
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Multiple distinct role definitions returned confirms RBAC is enabled; only a single default admin role confirms it is not.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the firewall management API to retrieve administrator role definitions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of multiple user entries with distinct role attributes (not all 'superuser') confirms RBAC is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the firewall administrative policy documentation to confirm whether RBAC has been formally configured and whether role assignments are reviewed periodically.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation showing role matrix and evidence of distinct role assignments confirms RBAC is enforced.

typical_values: false (RBAC not enabled; common in smaller organizations or default out-of-box configurations)
true (RBAC enforced with differentiated roles — recommended secure posture)

option_description: The total count of administrative accounts that have been assigned the full super-admin (unrestricted) role on the firewall management platform, representing the number of accounts with complete, unconstrained access.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Excessive Administrative Privilege Assignment' when rbac_enabled is true but admin_accounts_with_superadmin_role_count is 2 or greater and least_privilege_policy_enforced is false. A high count of super-admin accounts exponentially increases the attack surface: each additional full-privilege account is another credential that, if compromised, grants total firewall control. Best practice limits super-admin accounts to one or two break-glass emergency accounts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all administrative accounts and filter those assigned the super-admin or equivalent full-access role via CLI.
how_to_obtain.command: show admins | grep -i 'superuser\|superadmin\|full\|admin-role'; show running-config | grep -A2 'username' | grep -i 'privilege 15\|role superuser'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of accounts with super-admin designation; count the entries to get the total.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the administrator user list in the management console, filter by role, and count the accounts assigned the highest privilege or super-admin role.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management Console > Device > Administrators > filter by Role = Superuser or equivalent
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numerical count of accounts with the unrestricted super-admin role assignment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the management API to retrieve all admin accounts and their assigned roles, then count those with the superuser designation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer count reflecting the number of accounts with the superuser role attribute in the API response.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the firewall's running configuration file for admin account definitions and count those with privilege level 15 or super-admin role.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of accounts at maximum privilege level.

typical_values: 2-3 (small team sharing super-admin — common in SMB deployments)
5+ (widespread super-admin assignment — high-risk posture seen in unmanaged environments)

option_description: Indicates whether a documented and actively enforced least-privilege policy exists that restricts each administrative account to only the permissions required for its designated function, with super-admin reserved for break-glass or emergency use only.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this as a mitigating condition in the 'Excessive Administrative Privilege Assignment' rule: even when RBAC is enabled and super-admin count is 2 or more, the exposure is still triggered if least_privilege_policy_enforced is false. Without this policy, role assignments tend to drift toward over-privileged configurations over time, and there is no formal control preventing routine admin tasks from being performed with super-admin credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request and review the organization's firewall administration policy documentation to verify whether a least-privilege role assignment policy is formally documented, approved, and includes a review schedule.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented policy that specifies per-role permission scopes, prohibits routine use of super-admin for day-to-day tasks, and includes evidence of last review date.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review actual role assignments in the management console against each admin's documented job function to verify assignments are scoped to minimum required permissions.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management Console > Device > Administrators > review each account's assigned role against the role permission matrix
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each admin account's role matches the minimal permissions needed for their function; no routine-use accounts carry super-admin roles.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the firewall administrator or security team to determine whether super-admin accounts are used only for break-glass scenarios and whether role assignments are reviewed on a scheduled basis (e.g., quarterly).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that super-admin is not used for routine tasks, with evidence of a documented review cadence and access recertification records.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review firewall management audit logs to determine whether super-admin accounts are used for routine configuration changes rather than only emergency access, which would indicate the policy is not effectively enforced.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -i 'superadmin\|superuser' /var/log/firewall/audit.log | awk '{print $1,$2,$5,$7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Minimal entries for super-admin account activity; frequent routine operations logged under super-admin indicate the least-privilege policy is not enforced.

typical_values: false (no formal policy; super-admin used routinely — common in understaffed environments)
true (documented policy with scoped roles and periodic review — recommended secure posture)

option_description: Indicates whether the firewall performs stateful packet inspection by tracking TCP/UDP connection state and only permitting packets that correspond to an established session or valid new connection, blocking out-of-state or spoofed packets.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Missing Stateful Inspection Or Connection Tracking Disabled' directly when stateful_inspection_enabled is false. Without stateful inspection, the firewall cannot distinguish a legitimate mid-session packet from a crafted out-of-state attack packet. Attackers can inject TCP segments without completing a handshake, bypass rules that assume session context, or use protocol tunneling techniques that rely on the firewall accepting packets without state validation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux iptables-based firewalls, verify that conntrack-based state matching rules are present in the INPUT and FORWARD chains.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L -n -v | grep -E 'ESTABLISHED|RELATED|conntrack|state'; nft list ruleset | grep -E 'ct state|established|related'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules containing '-m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT' or 'ct state established,related accept' confirm stateful inspection is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether the conntrack kernel module is loaded and the connection tracking table is active.
how_to_obtain.command: lsmod | grep -i conntrack; conntrack -L | head -5; cat /proc/net/nf_conntrack | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Module listed in lsmod output and connection entries visible in the conntrack table confirm stateful tracking is operational.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On commercial firewall platforms, navigate to the security policy or firewall settings and verify that stateful inspection or connection tracking is enabled globally.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management Console > Configuration > Security Settings > Stateful Inspection / Connection Tracking (toggle or checkbox)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Setting shows 'Enabled' or equivalent affirmative state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the firewall rules configuration file for the presence of state-tracking rules or explicit disabling of connection tracking.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of ESTABLISHED/RELATED accept rules without any notrack/NOTRACK bypass entries confirms stateful inspection is enabled.

typical_values: true (stateful inspection active — default on most modern firewall platforms)
false (stateless operation; occasionally seen in high-throughput specialized appliances or misconfigured systems)

option_description: Defines the action the firewall takes when it receives packets that do not match any tracked connection state, such as TCP segments arriving without a preceding SYN, or mid-session packets with no corresponding session record in the state table.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Missing Stateful Inspection Or Connection Tracking Disabled' when invalid_state_packet_action is set to 'accept', even if stateful_inspection_enabled is true. Accepting invalid-state packets undermines the entire stateful inspection model: attackers can craft TCP packets that bypass stateful enforcement by exploiting the accept action for untracked traffic, enabling session hijacking, firewall rule bypass, and covert channel establishment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iptables-based firewalls, check for an explicit rule handling INVALID state packets and its target action.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v --line-numbers | grep INVALID; iptables -L FORWARD -n -v --line-numbers | grep INVALID
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A rule showing '-m state --state INVALID -j DROP' confirms invalid packets are dropped; absence of any INVALID rule or a target of ACCEPT indicates a misconfiguration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On nftables-based systems, check the ruleset for invalid connection tracking state handling.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ct state invalid drop' confirms secure handling; 'ct state invalid accept' or absence of the rule indicates exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the iptables persistent rules file for the INVALID state handling rule and its jump target.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: '-m state --state INVALID -j DROP' present indicates drop action is configured; absence or '-j ACCEPT' indicates the insecure accept posture.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On commercial firewall platforms, locate the invalid or out-of-state packet handling policy within the security zone or session settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management Console > Security Profiles > Zone Protection / Session Settings > Out-of-State Packet Handling
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Setting shows 'Drop', 'Log and Drop', or 'Reject' for invalid-state packets.

typical_values: drop (recommended default on most hardened deployments)
log_and_drop (used in security-conscious environments requiring audit trail of invalid packets)
accept (insecure; occasionally seen in permissively configured or legacy systems)
reject (less common; sends RST/ICMP unreachable in response)

option_description: Indicates whether an explicit bypass or exemption from stateful inspection has been configured to accommodate asymmetric routing paths, where outbound and return traffic traverse different firewall interfaces, which disables connection state validation for the affected traffic flows.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Missing Stateful Inspection Or Connection Tracking Disabled' whenever asymmetric_routing_bypass_enabled is true, regardless of whether stateful inspection is otherwise enabled. Asymmetric routing bypasses are frequently configured as a workaround for network topology issues but effectively create an uninspected traffic path. Attackers aware of this bypass can route malicious traffic through the exempted path to evade stateful enforcement entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based firewalls, check for NOTRACK rules or raw table entries that exempt traffic from connection tracking, which implements asymmetric bypass.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -t raw -L -n -v; nft list table ip raw 2>/dev/null; grep -r 'NOTRACK\|notrack\|CT --notrack' /etc/iptables/ /etc/nftables.conf 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of NOTRACK rules in the raw table for specific interfaces or subnets confirms asymmetric routing bypass is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search the firewall configuration for keywords indicating asymmetric routing exceptions or bypass policies.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any match confirms an asymmetric routing bypass or exemption is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the firewall's zone protection profiles or interface-level settings for asymmetric routing bypass or stateful inspection exemption options.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management Console > Network > Zones or Interfaces > select interface > Advanced Settings > Asymmetric Path / Bypass Stateful Inspection
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Setting shows 'Disabled' or 'None' to confirm bypass is not active; 'Enabled' or 'TCP Bypass' indicates the exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send a TCP packet with ACK flag but no preceding SYN through a suspected bypass path and observe whether the firewall accepts or drops it, indicating whether stateful enforcement is active on that path.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Dropped or no response indicates stateful inspection is enforced; a response from the target indicates the packet passed through uninspected.

typical_values: false (bypass disabled — recommended; default on properly designed network topologies)
true (bypass enabled — seen in environments with BGP asymmetric routing, load balancers without SNAT, or multi-ISP setups where topology corrections were deferred)

option_description: Indicates whether a redundant high-availability peer or cluster member is configured for the firewall, enabling automatic failover to a secondary unit in the event of hardware failure, software crash, or planned maintenance.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'No High Availability Or Failover Configuration' when ha_peer_configured is false. A single firewall with no HA peer is a single point of failure for all network traffic it governs. Beyond availability loss, fail-open configurations on devices without HA can result in all traffic passing uninspected during an outage, creating a complete security bypass. Attackers may intentionally trigger device instability to force a fail-open condition.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On firewall CLI, check the HA or clustering configuration status to determine if a peer is defined and synchronized.
how_to_obtain.command: show high-availability all; show ha state; show failover; show cluster status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing a peer IP address, synchronization state, and active/passive or active/active role assignment confirms HA is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the HA or cluster configuration section of the firewall management console to verify peer configuration and link status.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management Console > Device > High Availability > General (or equivalent vendor path) — verify Peer HA IP address is defined and link state shows 'Up' or 'Synchronized'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A populated peer IP field and an active synchronization or heartbeat status confirms ha_peer_configured is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the firewall management API to retrieve the HA configuration and peer status.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response containing peer-info elements with a valid IP address and 'state' indicating 'passive' or 'active' confirms HA peer is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the firewall's running configuration for HA stanza entries defining a peer address and failover parameters.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A stanza containing a peer IP address, heartbeat interface, and failover trigger conditions confirms HA peer is configured.

typical_values: false (no HA peer; common in small business, branch office, or cost-constrained deployments)
true (HA peer configured — standard in enterprise, data center, and service provider environments)

option_description: Controls the firewall's behavior upon hardware or software failure: fail-open allows all traffic to pass without inspection, fail-closed drops all traffic, and none means no failover mechanism is defined at all.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags an exposure when ha_peer_configured is true but failover_mode is fail_open, or when failover_mode is none and no HA peer exists. A fail-open configuration means any crash or failure silently removes all enforcement, allowing unrestricted traffic flow. This directly enables T1599 Network Boundary Bridging and T1562.013 Disable or Modify Network Device Firewall, as an attacker who can force a firewall fault gains unimpeded network access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iptables/nftables Linux firewalls, check kernel netfilter failover policy and any HA daemon configuration such as Keepalived or Corosync.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf 2>/dev/null; systemctl status corosync pacemaker 2>/dev/null; grep -r 'fail' /etc/firewalld/ /etc/ufw/ 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows defined VRRP or cluster state with an explicit 'nopreempt' or 'fail_close' directive; absence of any HA configuration indicates failover_mode of none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Palo Alto Networks: navigate to Device > High Availability > General. Review the Failure Condition and Link Monitoring settings to determine whether the device fails open or closed.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Device > High Availability > General > Failure Condition
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Panel shows 'HA Enabled' with Failure Condition set to 'fail-closed' or equivalent; if HA is disabled the failover_mode is none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Palo Alto Panorama or device REST API for HA configuration details.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: XML response includes <enabled>yes</enabled> with <state> showing active/passive and a <passive-link-state> field; fail-open is indicated by passive-link-state set to auto or shutdown absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Cisco ASA, inspect the running configuration for 'failover' statements and the 'failover policy' directive.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Failover On' with 'failover lan' and 'failover link' lines indicates active/standby HA; absence of any failover line confirms failover_mode none.

typical_values: fail_closed (recommended; drop all traffic on failure)
fail_open (found in environments prioritizing uptime over security)

option_description: Indicates whether ICMP traffic is permitted inbound from untrusted or external zones without any source IP restriction or rate limiting applied at the firewall rule level.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the icmp_and_diagnostic_service_overexposure exposure whenever this attribute is true. Unrestricted inbound ICMP allows external actors to perform host discovery and network mapping (T1018 Remote System Discovery, T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery) without authentication. Ping sweeps, ICMP timestamp requests, and address mask requests all reveal live hosts and network topology. Without rate limiting, ICMP floods can also contribute to denial-of-service conditions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On an iptables firewall, list all rules that permit ICMP and check whether any source restriction (-s) is applied.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v --line-numbers | grep -i icmp; ip6tables -L INPUT -n -v --line-numbers | grep -i icmp
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules permitting ICMP should show a specific source CIDR in the 'source' column; a value of '0.0.0.0/0' or 'anywhere' with no rate-limit match (-m limit) indicates inbound_icmp_unrestricted is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect saved iptables rules or nftables configuration for ICMP permit entries and check for hashlimit or limit modules.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines matching 'ACCEPT' for icmp without '-m limit' or '-s <trusted_cidr>' confirm unrestricted ICMP ingress.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform an ICMP probe from an external or untrusted test host to confirm reachability and measure whether rate limiting is enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If all 100 rapid pings receive replies without packet loss, no rate limiting is present; any reply to the hping3 flood confirms fail-open ICMP policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Cisco FMC or FTD: navigate to Policies > Access Control, filter rules by ICMP application or port, and examine source zone and source network conditions on any ICMP-permit rule.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Policies > Access Control > <Policy Name> > Filter by Application: ICMP
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Source zone should be a trusted or specific zone; source network should be a named object rather than 'any'. Rules showing zone=any and network=any confirm the attribute is true.

typical_values: false (secure baseline; ICMP restricted to trusted sources or rate-limited)
true (common in legacy or unmanaged deployments where ICMP was never restricted)

option_description: Indicates whether SNMP traffic on UDP/161 (queries) and UDP/162 (traps) is permitted inbound from untrusted or external zones without a source IP allowlist or authentication enforcement at the firewall rule level.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers icmp_and_diagnostic_service_overexposure when this value is true. Exposed SNMP from untrusted zones enables T1602.001 SNMP MIB Dump, allowing attackers to enumerate the full network topology, interface configurations, routing tables, and device inventory without any prior authentication if the community string is known or guessable. SNMPv1/v2c community strings transmitted over UDP are trivially intercepted, and writable community strings can alter device configurations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check iptables or nftables for ACCEPT rules on UDP port 161 and 162 and verify whether a source IP restriction is applied.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v | grep -E ':161|:162'; nft list ruleset | grep -E 'udp dport (161|162)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing ACCEPT for dpt:161 or dpt:162 without a source CIDR restriction indicate inbound_snmp_unrestricted is true; any rule with a specific source IP range is acceptable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt an SNMP walk from an untrusted network segment using a common community string to validate reachability.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A successful walk returning OID data confirms SNMP is reachable without firewall restriction; a timeout or 'No response' confirms SNMP is blocked.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Palo Alto Networks: navigate to Policies > Security and filter rules by application 'snmp'. Review the source zone and source address for any permit rule.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Policies > Security > Filter by Application: snmp
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Source zone should not include untrusted or external zones; source address should not be 'any'. If source is 'any' from an external zone, attribute is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the Cisco ASA or IOS access control list entries governing SNMP access via the 'snmp-server community' and associated ACLs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'snmp-server community <string> ro <acl-name>' with a defined ACL restricting source IPs is secure; absence of an ACL reference or use of 'permit any' in the referenced ACL confirms the attribute is true.

typical_values: false (recommended; SNMP restricted to NMS IP addresses via ACL)
true (observed in environments where SNMP was enabled for monitoring without subsequent firewall tightening)

option_description: An array listing diagnostic or management protocols beyond ICMP and SNMP that are permitted inbound from untrusted zones without restriction, such as traceroute (UDP/33434-33534), NTP (UDP/123), CDP, LLDP, or inbound syslog.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers icmp_and_diagnostic_service_overexposure whenever this array contains one or more entries. Each protocol in the list represents a distinct reconnaissance or amplification vector: traceroute reveals hop-by-hop network topology (T1016), NTP on UDP/123 can be abused for amplification attacks or used to enumerate NTP peers, CDP and LLDP leak device model and software version details to adjacent-segment attackers, and inbound syslog can be spoofed to inject false log entries. A non-empty array means the firewall permits at least one of these protocols from untrusted zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate iptables rules permitting UDP ports associated with diagnostic protocols from external or untrusted sources.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v | grep -E 'dpt:123|dpt:33[0-9]{3}|dpt:514'; iptables -L INPUT -n -v | grep -E 'dpt:2055|dpt:4739'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACCEPT rules on these ports without source CIDR restrictions confirm entries that should be added to the diagnostic_protocols_exposed array; no output means the protocols are blocked.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run a UDP port scan from an untrusted test host targeting the firewall's external interface on diagnostic protocol ports to confirm reachability.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Ports reported as 'open' or 'open|filtered' indicate those protocols are reachable and should be listed in the array; 'closed' or 'filtered' means properly blocked.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review nftables ruleset or Cisco ASA access-list for permit statements covering diagnostic UDP/TCP ports from any source.
how_to_obtain.command: nft list ruleset | grep -E 'udp dport \{123, 514, 33434|33440\}'; show access-list | include permit udp any
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Permit statements matching these port ranges from source 'any' or an untrusted subnet confirm the protocol should be included in the exposed list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the network operations team to determine whether any monitoring integrations require inbound NTP, syslog, or CDP from external segments, and review change tickets for rule justifications.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented business justification with time-limited approval and source IP restriction for each exposed protocol; absence of documentation or source restrictions confirms unrestricted exposure.

typical_values: [] (secure baseline; no diagnostic protocols exposed from untrusted zones)
['traceroute'] (common in environments where ISP or NOC traceroute is permitted)
['ntp', 'traceroute'] (seen when NTP sync from internet sources is allowed without restriction)
['ntp', 'traceroute', 'syslog_inbound'] (found in misconfigured environments where monitoring was set up without zone controls)
